results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

Every outline summary of a body unit agrees with the controlling idea of its aligned spec paragraph, in spec order (p01-p67, with the worked example after channels and p57 inside the Chief Architect's View); the five callouts have no spec paragraph and are not counted.

The outliner marked two units two_ideas: Introduction ¶3 (terms owned plus the chapters it builds on) and Vertical Differences ¶1 (canonical-property alerts plus automotive feed lag). Each realises a spec paragraph (p03, p59) whose controlling idea joins exactly these parts, and the draft states one governing idea for each (the chapter's scope; 'alert quality depends on systems outside the alert platform'). No other unit was marked.

Every body unit ties to a supporting claim: scene to S2/S3/S5, concepts to S1/S3, matching and sizing to S2, architecture to S1-S3, fan-out, channels and consent to S3/S4, liquidity and risk gate to S5, taxonomy to S6, the closing sections to all six. No unit is off-thesis.

Figures 1-6 each carry a caption stating what they show; the baseline, four-parts, channel, metrics and trade-offs tables are introduced or followed by a sentence giving their point; the Rightmove/Homegate list carries its caveat; the Elastic constraints are read in 'Point 4 matters...' and constraint 2's projection consequence; FCM quotas, Gmail rules and leboncoin are each followed by what they mean for Veldmark; the productscape quotations and the Eixample case are interpreted. Exception reported separately: the vertical table.

results.quote: Beyond the table, two verticals show that alert quality depends on systems outside the alert platform.
results.finding: The vertical table follows the heading with no lead-in and no sentence saying what it shows (the spec's 'Tuning differs by vertical', the section idea that saved-search shape, speed sensitivity, channels, duplicates, fraud and taxonomy churn change how alerts are tuned). The only following sentence moves 'beyond the table' to two cases, so the table's own point is left to the reader.

All other boundaries express the declared relationship and pick up the declared known information, notably: 'At Veldmark ... the obligation covers' (example), 'On Tuesday morning ... still feature the bike' (contrast), 'Veldmark's 2027 baseline numbers show the bike is typical' (additional support), 'The design rule follows' (cause_effect), 'Once fan-out has decided who is notified and when' (sequence), 'To size this design' (sequence), 'The cost buys speed' (cause_effect), 'Beyond capacity, the order ... is a fairness decision' (contrast), 'Every minute of hold costs honest sellers' (contrast), 'That pipeline now puts...' and '... is therefore the work of the next part' (cause_effect); the hand-off links [[part-5]] and [[trust-and-safety-architecture]]. Section openers for matching, fan-out, taxonomy and consent pick up their predecessor only through the heading or a shared key word; judged adequate, not material.

The introduction opens on concrete saved searches (bike, Lyon T3, Golf) and the obligation they create, then Veldmark's scale, the owned terms and a roadmap; none of placeholder, restated question, dictionary, 'dawn of man' or book report.

The conclusion does not open with 'in conclusion', introduces no new subtopic (Part V is a hand-off), holds no body evidence beyond callbacks, and is more than a rephrased thesis: it joins the six Part IV surfaces and draws the speed/fraud consequence.

It states what no section states: the six Part IV chapters form one pipeline answering the part's three questions (availability, who decided position, contact), and says why it matters: that speed is worth as much to a fraudster as to an honest seller, so it is safe only behind a risk gate and decisions every surface obeys.

The last section shows how the six surfaces fit together, answers the Part IV opening's three questions for discovery as a whole, returns to Femke's seven-minute first contact and the 180 Eixample rentals with about 41,000 alerts, and hands off to Part V and [[trust-and-safety-architecture]] through the risk alerts carry.

The intro reader predicts the sections in roadmap order (scene with Femke's bike and the cron job; saved searches, match sets and watchers; percolation versus re-querying; store with rebuildable percolators; fan-out and channels; sizing; liquidity, risk gate, taxonomy, consent; trade-offs, verticals, failure modes, Chief Architect's view, questions; Part IV close), the evidence (fictional Veldmark, Rightmove and Homegate, metrics, named failure patterns) and a declarative, practitioner tone. It does not foresee engine documentation or trade press beyond the portals, a minor gap against expected.

The AC-1 reader states the expected design: saved-search store of record with normalized versioned queries and rebuildable percolators partitioned with pre-filters; reverse matching on listing events with notify-on-entry and a match ledger; a notification orchestrator with deduplication, caps, quiet hours and randomized order; retraction plus a send-time availability check for digests; a trust-and-safety risk gate keeping risky listings not alertable, stricter in rentals, with a short hold for new accounts; and measurement by alert latency (5 minutes p95 searchable to provider), ghost-alert rate, alert-to-contact, unsubscribes and dormant share, explicitly not sends.
